Using the stated assumptions—6% account growth, 2.5% inflation, no state income tax, heirs’ 10% tax rate on inherited pre-tax IRAs, and the 2026–2050 projection window—the projected after-tax wealth in 2026 dollars is:

- **Option C (no conversion):** $2,513,140  
- **Option A ($190,000/year conversions):** $2,516,844  
- **Option B ($195,500/year conversions):** $2,512,691  

Option A leaves the most after-tax wealth, beating no conversion by about $3,704. Option B is slightly worse than doing nothing, by about $450.

For **N1**, 2026 federal income tax is projected at $4,665 under C and $41,855 under B, a difference of **$37,190**.

For **N2**, 2028 Medicare premiums are projected at $2,558 per person under C and $3,764 per person under B. For two people, that is $5,116 versus $7,528, a difference of **$2,412**.

## What the projection shows

All three plans were run through the same 2026–2050 projection (5% return, 2.5% inflation, Frank's death in 2032, survivor spending unchanged, heirs' IRA dollars taxed at 22%, everything in 2026 dollars).

| Plan | Lifetime federal tax | Lifetime Medicare | After-tax wealth at end (today's $) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **C — no conversions** | $1,264,674 | $246,361 | **$3,072,664** |
| **A — convert 2033–2038** | $1,167,072 | $224,694 | **$3,144,173** (+$71,510) |
| **B — convert 2026–2031** | $931,696 | $200,357 | **$3,328,935** (+$256,272) |

**Why B wins.** The decisive fact is the 2032 death. Option A's conversions land in 2033–2038, when Joyce is filing **single** and already pulling RMDs off Frank's $2.4M IRA — the engine shows each A conversion year costing roughly $82,000 of federal tax ("taxed at the 24% and 32% and 35% brackets") and pushing her to IRMAA tier 4. Option B converts while the joint brackets are still available: 2026 costs $33,282 of tax on the extra $155,000 ("taxed at the 10% and 12% and 22% brackets"), and the same money is never taxed again. By 2031 Joyce's traditional IRA is essentially emptied ($153,683 left), so her post-2032 RMDs collapse and the survivor is never again pushed into the top brackets. That shows up in both ledgers: lifetime tax is $332,977 lower than doing nothing, and lifetime Medicare $46,004 lower.

**C** is the weakest: it keeps the RMD spiral going, and from 2035 on Joyce sits in IRMAA tier 3–4 with federal tax climbing to $105,332 by 2050, plus ~$2M of pre-tax IRA still left for heirs at 22%.

**Caveats worth flagging.** These conversions come only from Joyce's IRA; Frank's $1.79M IRA (with $153,000 of basis, so partly tax-free pro rata) is untouched and is what drives the survivor's bracket risk. If the heirs are in the 32% bracket rather than 22%, converting pays even more (the engine's sensitivity puts the gain $46,589 higher). A 7% return would add roughly $289,279 to the value of converting.

**N1 — 2026 federal tax, B vs C:** $33,282 − $1,041 = $32,241. The extra $155,000 lifts taxable Social Security from $36,413 to $59,976 ("tax torpedo") and shrinks the senior deduction from $12,000 to $1,623.

**N2 — 2028 Medicare, B vs C:** Under C both spouses pay the standard $2,558 ($213.20 × 12). Under B, 2026 MAGI of $259,476 puts both in the first joint IRMAA tier: $3,764 each ($298.50 + $15.20 = $313.70 × 12). Total $7,528 vs $5,116 = **$2,412**.

PICK: B
N1: 32241
N2: 2412

text:
## The short answer: both claims are true, but they're not the same size

**Claim 1 — "the next few years are a good time to convert":** yes. **Claim 2 — "converting costs them the senior deduction":** also yes, but that cost is a small slice of the pie.

### What the 2026 return actually looks like

Under **B (no conversion)**, 2026 has Ken's RMD of $38,039, Social Security of $54,600 (of which $46,410 is taxable), savings interest and dividends: AGI **$112,503**, taxable income $65,003, federal tax **$6,620**, and the full senior deduction **$12,000**.

Under **C**, the $65,000 conversion is only partly taxable — Ken's Form 8606 basis of $131,000 makes about $56,719 of it ordinary income. That lifts AGI to **$169,221**, and here's the exact anatomy of the extra **$9,691**:

| Piece | Cost |
|---|---|
| Extra ordinary income taxed at 12%/22% | +$8,328 |
| Senior deduction shrinking from $12,000 to **$9,693** (6% of the $19,221 MAGI excess, per spouse) | +$507 |
| Qualified dividends pushed out of the 0% band | +$855 |

So the deduction loss is **$507 of a $9,691 bill — about 5%.** The "conversion kills the senior deduction" worry is real but it's a rounding error next to the bracket tax. (Note the deduction expires after 2028 anyway, which is exactly why Option A's 2029–2031 conversions forgo it entirely — and why the 2026–2028 window is the one worth using.)

The good news: MAGI of $169,221 stays under the first joint IRMAA tier ($218,000), so **none of the three plans ever pays a Medicare surcharge** — lifetime Medicare is $166,339 in all three.

### Why C still wins

| | After-tax wealth, end of 2050 (2026 dollars) |
|---|---|
| **C — convert 2026–2028** | **$3,243,317** |
| A — convert 2029–2031 | $3,216,465 |
| B — no conversions | $3,170,788 |

- **C beats A by $26,852**, and C beats B by $72,529. Not close enough to call it a tie.
- Lifetime federal tax: C $654,249 vs. A $681,793 vs. B $766,320 (today's dollars: $454,362 / $473,913 / $520,452).
- The mechanics: C front-loads conversions while the 12% bracket and the senior deduction are still available, and it shrinks the traditional IRAs enough that later RMDs — which climb to $117,204 by 2050 under B — are taxed in a lower bracket. Every year from 2034 on, B pays roughly $3,000–$10,800 more tax than A, and by 2039+ the NIIT kicks in on top (B reaches $6,627 of NIIT in 2050).
- A is better than doing nothing but worse than C: it converts at 22% with no senior deduction to protect and after three more years of RMD-driven growth.

### What would change the answer
The engine's biggest lever is the **return assumption** (at 8% the payoff grows by about $27,753) and, second, **the heirs' bracket** — a 10% heir rate is what the conventions specify; at 32% converting is worth $754 more. Health/longevity moves it by about $3,951.

PICK: C
N1: 9691
N2: 9693

## What the numbers say

**The household, as I modeled it:** MFJ, no state income tax, Ray (b. Feb 1957, age 69) and Linda (b. Sept 1959, age 67), both on Medicare with Part B + Part D, both already on Social Security at FRA ($3,460 + $1,180/mo = $55,680 for 2026). Assets: Ray's traditional IRA $1.6M with $208,000 of Form 8606 basis, Linda's traditional IRA $60,000, two Roth IRAs, $440,000 joint cash earning 5% (plus Linda's $9,000 taxable interest and Ray's $6,000 of muni interest). Spending $92,000 after tax, $4,500 of property tax as the only itemized item, 2024 MAGI $104,000 and 2025 MAGI $150,000 for the first two years of IRMAA. After-tax wealth measured at the end of 2050 in 2026 dollars, with pre-tax IRAs discounted at the 12% heirs' rate.

**Why the answer isn't "convert as much as possible."** Ray's IRA is large enough that RMDs alone (starting 2030, age 73) plus Social Security already push them into the 22% bracket for the rest of their lives — so converting at 22% now is roughly a wash, and the real money is in three cheaper stretches and three cliffs:

- **Cheapest dollars first.** The first ~$19,150 of 2026 conversion costs only 10.5¢ per dollar (12% bracket, before the Social Security "tax torpedo" finishes); everything up to ~$67,300 is still only 10.5¢.
- **The tax torpedo.** Their Social Security is not yet 85% taxable at baseline, so early conversion dollars drag extra benefits into income. Once taxable SS hits the 85% cap (47,328), that surcharge disappears.
- **The senior deduction cliff.** The OBBBA $6,000-per-person deduction (worth $12,000 in 2026) phases out at 6% of MAGI over $150,000 and is fully gone at about $183,400 of 2026 income — an effective +6 points on a band of conversion dollars.
- **The IRMAA cliff at ~$230,000 of 2028 MAGI.** A big conversion in 2026 lifts 2028 Part B + Part D by $2,412 for the couple. Pushing past that cliff for a couple of thousand extra converted dollars destroys value.
- **The pro-rata rule softens everything.** Because $208,000 of the $1.6M is after-tax basis, only ~87.6% of each conversion is taxable ($118,000 converts with $103,390 taxable), which is why the break points sit at higher gross amounts than you'd expect.

**The search.** Flat amounts from $0 to $400,000 a year for 1 to 10 years were each run through the full 2026–2050 projection. The curve peaks in the $105,000–$120,000 band over 8–10 years:

| Plan | After-tax wealth vs. doing nothing (2026 $) |
|---|---|
| **$118,000 × 8 (2026–2033)** | **+$134,445** |
| $153,600 × 6 ("stay under the 2028 IRMAA tier") | +$133,853 |
| $105,000 × 10 | +$132,630 |
| $110,000 × 8 | +$132,264 |
| $120,000 × 8 | +$131,481 |
| $180,100 × 5 (fill the 22% bracket) | +$113,020 |
| $155,000 × 1 (the N1/N2 question) | +$30,654 |

$118,000 × 8 converts $944,000 in total, cuts lifetime federal tax by about $254,000 in today's dollars, costs **nothing** extra in Medicare premiums (MAGI stays under every IRMAA tier in every year), and leaves roughly $775,000 still in Ray's IRA at the end versus $1.54M if they do nothing. It's a close call — $110,000 × 8 is only $2,181 behind and $105,000 × 10 is $1,815 behind — so if you'd rather not cut it that fine, $110,000 × 8 is a very defensible plan.

**N1 — the 2026 tax cost of a single $155,000 conversion.** With no conversion their 2026 federal tax is **$2,812** (AGI $75,064, taxable SS $33,064, taxable income $27,564). Converting $155,000 on December 31, 2026 — $135,810 taxable after the 12.38% basis share — lifts AGI to $225,138, taxable SS to the 85% cap of $47,328, cuts the senior deduction from $12,000 to $2,984, and produces federal tax of **$30,488**. The difference is **$27,676**: $22,554 of bracket tax, $3,138 of tax torpedo, $1,984 of lost senior deduction.

**N2 — the 2028 Medicare bill for that same one-time conversion.** 2026 MAGI becomes $231,138, which crosses the 2028 joint tier-1 threshold of $230,000. Instead of $213.20 × 12 = $2,558 each, they pay $298.50 + $15.20 = $313.70 × 12 = $3,764 each. That's $1,206 per spouse × 2 = **$2,412** for the year.

**Caveats worth flagging.** The 12% heirs' rate is your convention; if the kids are in the 32% bracket the optimum moves up to about $220,000 a year, and at a 7% return it moves to about $180,000 a year — so the heirs' bracket and the actual investment mix are the two facts that would most change the answer. Also, I could not give the $6,000 of tax-exempt muni interest its proper effect inside the Social Security worksheet, so the taxable-SS figures are marginally understated (a few hundred dollars a year at most).

PLAN: 118000 x 8
N1: 27676
N2: 2412

## What the numbers show

**The RMD first.** Lou was born in 1953, so his required beginning age is 73 (SECURE 2.0), and he turns 73 in 2026 — this is his first RMD year. The Uniform Lifetime Table divisor for age 73 is 26.5, so his 2026 RMD is $1,570,000 ÷ 26.5 = **$59,245** (the tool returns 59,245.28). Edie is also 73 in 2026, so she has one too: $390,000 ÷ 26.5 = $14,717. Household RMD = $73,962. Because they take it in 2026 rather than deferring to April 2027, it is ordinary income on the 2026 return and it is *not* eligible for conversion — the conversion in every option sits on top of the RMD (option A's Lou IRA goes 1,570,000 × 1.05 − 59,245 RMD − 260,000 conversion = 1,329,255).

**The three outcomes** (after-tax wealth at the end of 2050, in today's dollars):

| Option | After-tax wealth | vs. B |
|---|---|---|
| B: RMD only | $3,084,611 | — |
| **A: RMD + $260k in 2026–27** | **$3,195,553** | **+$110,943** |
| C: RMD + $75k in 2026–31 | $3,188,393 | +$103,782 |

A wins by $7,161 over C — outside the $1,000 "close call" band, so it's a genuine pick, though not a landslide.

**Why A wins.** B leaves the IRAs to compound: RMDs keep climbing ($73,962 → $164,484), and by 2049–2050 the couple is pushed into IRMAA tier 1 with premiums of $6,323–$6,481 each. A converts at 22–24% in two big bites (2026 taxable income $374,484, still inside the 24% bracket), which cuts lifetime federal tax by $222,388 and keeps them in IRMAA tier 0 from 2030 on. The price is two years of tier‑3 premiums in 2028–2029 ($7,412 and $7,597 each, set by the 2026 and 2027 MAGI of $415,984 and $410,613) and no senior deduction in those years — net Medicare cost +$11,450. C spreads it thinner: six years of 22% conversions, IRMAA tier 1 in 2028–29, and it never fully drains the traditional balance, so the later-life RMD drag stays larger.

**The 2026 tax cost of C.** Under B the 2026 return shows AGI $149,984, taxable income $102,484, federal tax **$11,350**. Under C the extra $75,000 lifts AGI to $224,984, shrinks the senior deduction from $12,000 to $3,002, and pushes the qualified dividends out of the 0% band (they sit on top of $178,232 of ordinary income), giving taxable income $186,482 and federal tax **$29,873**. The difference is **$18,523** — which is exactly the year-one "why" line for C.

**Caveats worth knowing:** this ranking is return-sensitive — at a 3% return the tool says C would become the best (A's edge would shrink), and if the heirs are in the 12% bracket the case for converting weakens. Both are worth confirming. But on the facts given, A is the answer.

PICK: A

text:
## What the projection shows

**Timing of Social Security (A vs. B).** Both claiming at 67 leaves **$2,625,461** in today's dollars; Sam waiting to 70 leaves **$2,641,584**. Waiting is worth only about **$16,000** — small, because Sam's larger benefit is the one that carries over to Pat as a survivor benefit, but eight extra years of drawing on the portfolio offsets most of the gain. Note the projection also shows Sam's 2031 benefit is $59,376 under B versus $47,880 under A.

**Roth conversions (C).** Converting $180,000 a year in 2026–2029 leaves **$2,812,226** — about **$170,642 more than B** and **$186,765 more than A**. The conversions are cheap precisely because Sam has not yet claimed: with no Social Security on the return, 2026 taxable income with the conversion is $150,807, still inside the 22% bracket (which runs to $211,400), and the tax is $22,255 — an effective rate near 14% on the converted amount because Sam's $163,000 of Form 8606 basis makes part of each conversion tax-free (only $155,931 of the $180,000 is taxable in 2026). Lifetime federal tax drops from $612,557 (B) to $370,472 (C), and lifetime Medicare premiums fall from $169,756 to $131,290, because a smaller pre-tax IRA means smaller RMDs after 2035 and a survivor who never climbs into the upper IRMAA tiers (in B, Pat's single-filer premiums hit tier 2 and 3 from 2043 on).

## Answers

**N1.** 2026 federal tax: B = $0 (AGI $37,200 is fully absorbed by the $35,500 standard deduction plus the $12,000 senior deduction); C = $22,255. Difference = **$22,255**.

**N2.** Under B, Sam claims at 70 (February 2030), so 2031 is a full benefit year: **$59,376**.

**Caveats worth flagging:** the brokerage account's titling wasn't stated (the projection assumed a step-up, a ±$6,000 effect), and the answer is sensitive to spending — at $134,400 a year instead of $112,000, option B would edge out C, because the conversions would leave less liquid money to fund spending.

PICK: C
N1: 22255
N2: 59376

## What the projection shows

**The setup that matters.** Pat's inherited IRA must be gone by 12/31/2033. Because the parent died in 2023 *after* their required beginning date, Pat owes an annual RMD in 2026–2032 and then the entire remaining balance in 2033 — so all three options take out essentially the same dollars; the only difference is *when* they hit the return and what rate they pay.

**N1 — the 2026 inherited-IRA RMD.** The engine applies the 10-year rule with annual RMDs: prior year-end balance of $510,000 divided by Pat's single life-expectancy factor for age 67 → **$24,402** (and it confirms this: $510,000 × 1.06 − $24,402 = $516,198, the reported year-end balance). Pat's own IRA and Sam's IRA have no RMDs yet (RMD age 73 → 2031 and 2032).

**After-tax wealth at the end of 2050 (2026 dollars, pre-tax IRAs haircut at 32%):**

| Plan | After-tax wealth | vs. B | Lifetime federal tax | Lifetime Medicare |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **C** — RMD + $55k/yr 2026–2033 | **$4,721,638** | **+$12,884** | $1,652,491 | $277,958 |
| B — RMD only, lump at 2033 | $4,708,755 | — | $1,679,019 | $283,898 |
| A — RMD + $200k in 2026 & 2027 | $4,686,489 | −$22,266 | $1,637,477 | $287,503 |

**Why C wins.** Under B, $553,600 of inherited IRA lands in one year, pushing 2033 into the 24%/32%/35% brackets and into IRMAA tier 4 two years later (Part B+D of $10,978 per person vs. $2,894 at tier 0). Under A you pay 2026–27 at an even worse rate — the $200,000 knocks out the whole $12,000 senior deduction, pushes the qualified dividends out of the 0% band, adds NIIT ($1,486 in 2026, $1,897 in 2027) and puts them in IRMAA tier 2 in 2028–29 — and you *still* face a $126,688 lump in 2033. C smooths the distributions so the early years are taxed mostly at 12%/22% with Social Security already at its 85% ceiling, and it shrinks the 2033 spike to $146,526. The cost per dollar of the C withdrawal in 2026 is about 25 cents — cheaper than the 24%–35% + IRMAA that the 2033 lump costs under B. (The $55k withdrawal is "clamped" in 2033, when the account runs dry — that's the deadline being met exactly.)

**N2 — 2026 federal tax, C vs. B.** Same income both ways except the extra $55,000: pension $34,000 + Pat's interest $8,500 + savings interest $15,600 + RMD $24,402 + non-qualified dividends $3,750 = $86,252 ordinary, plus $11,250 qualified dividends and $51,612 of taxable Social Security. B = **$10,754.78**; C = **$24,520.19** (the extra income shrinks the senior deduction from $12,000 to $5,506 and pushes all $11,250 of gains from 0% to 15%). Difference ≈ **$13,765**.

C is ahead of B by $12,884 and ahead of A by $35,149 — comfortably more than the $1,000 "close call" band. The follow-ups (muni interest, an 8% return, heirs' bracket) move the numbers but not the ranking.

PICK: C
N1: 24402
N2: 13765

text:
## What the projection can and cannot tell you

I ran their plan exactly as given (the $100,000 conversion in 2026, 6% on every account, spending $139,000 rising with inflation, RMDs starting for Gus in 2027, Irene's already running, IRMAA set by the 2024/2025 returns). At the end of 2036 the Roth IRAs come out at:

- Gus's Roth: **$283,491**
- Irene's Roth: **$37,966**
- Combined: **$321,457**

That number is identical for option A and option B, and that is the whole problem. The planning convention applies one return — 6% — to every account. It has no way to know that a total stock market index fund and a high-dividend equity fund earn different returns, so it will report a $0 difference between them no matter how the comparison is set up. Running it twice would just print the same $321,457 twice.

## The part of the question that *can* be answered

Inside a Roth IRA, the dividend question is a non-issue on the tax side. Dividends are reinvested and grow tax-free, exactly like price appreciation, and there is no 0%/15%/20% capital-gain rate, no NIIT, no "tax torpedo" and no RMD on the Roth. So the usual reason a high-dividend fund is shunned — it throws off taxable income every year — simply doesn't exist here. The choice collapses to one thing: **which fund has the higher total return, net of fees.**

On that, the general case favors **A**, for reasons that aren't in the data I was given but are well established:
- A total stock market index fund is the whole market, cap-weighted, at a few basis points of cost. A high-dividend fund is a screened slice — typically large-cap value, sector-tilted toward utilities, staples, energy and REITs — so it gives up diversification and usually carries a higher expense ratio.
- A dividend screen explicitly excludes the non-payers and low-payers, which is where a large share of long-run total return has historically come from. Total return = dividends + growth; the high-dividend fund buys the first term at the cost of the second.
- Over a 10-year window (2026–2036), the compounding gap between, say, a 7% and a 6% total return on a ~$321,000 balance is tens of thousands of dollars — but I cannot state which gap is right without the two funds' expected returns.

## Why I can't give you N1

The dollar gap in 2036 depends entirely on the two funds' expected total returns, expense ratios, and how the dividend yield interacts with growth — none of which are in the facts. The $100,000 conversion, the existing $55,000 and $20,000 Roth balances, and the 6% convention pin down the *balance* (about $321,457 combined at the end of 2036) but say nothing about the *spread* between two different funds. Any number I put on N1 would be invented, and a fabricated figure is worse than none for a decision about where a six-figure sum gets invested.

Two things would settle it: the expected total return (or the expense ratios plus a yield/growth assumption) for each candidate fund, and whether Gus's Roth will be spent, inherited, or left to compound past 2036 — the last matters because a surviving spouse or heir inherits a Roth tax-free, which keeps the "total return is all that counts" logic intact to the end.

The one thing I'd say without reservation: whatever the model's indifference suggests, A is the better default inside the Roth, and the choice should be made on cost and diversification, not on yield.

PICK: CANT

text:
## What the muni bonds actually do

Before the numbers, one correction to the premise: the $24,000 of municipal interest is *not* invisible to this decision. It's out of AGI, but it goes back into **provisional income** on the Pub 915 worksheet (so it makes Social Security taxable) and into **MAGI for IRMAA** (so it sets Medicare premiums two years later). Under "do nothing" it already drags 44,590 of the 63,000 of benefits into income.

## The three runs (2026–2050, 6% return, 32% heirs' rate, today's dollars)

| | Lifetime tax | Lifetime Medicare | After-tax wealth end of 2050 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **C — no conversion** | 523,672 | 133,230 | **3,328,602** |
| **B — convert 126,500** | 489,629 | 128,634 | **3,386,455** |
| **A — convert 135,500** | 487,507 | 128,634 | **3,389,555** |

A beats B by 3,100 and C by 60,953 — outside the $1,000 "close call" band, so A.

Why: the conversion is 96% taxable (Walt's 46,000 of basis spread over a 1,144,800 IRA after 2026 growth → 130,055 of the 135,500 is taxable), and it is taxed at only 12%/22%. In exchange it permanently shrinks IRAs that would otherwise push RMDs into the 22%–24% bracket plus NIIT from 2032 onward — the "why" shows tax savings of roughly 2,000–8,000 a year from 2032 to 2050, and it drops them out of the first IRMAA tier in 2046–2048 (worth about 3,800 a year).

## N1 — extra 2026 federal tax, A vs C

| 2026 | C | A |
|---|---|---|
| AGI | 78,490 | 217,505 |
| Taxable SS | 44,590 | 53,550 (85% cap) |
| Senior deduction | 12,000 | 3,899 |
| Taxable income | 30,990 | 178,106 |
| **Federal tax** | **2,964** | **28,456** |

Difference: 28,456 − 2,964 = **25,492** (the engine's year-2026 bridge: +21,415 brackets, +1,971 tax torpedo, +1,782 senior-deduction phase-out, +324 dividends pushed out of the 0% band).

## N2 — extra 2028 Medicare premiums, A vs C

2028 premiums are set by 2026 MAGI. Option C's 2026 MAGI is 102,490 → standard tier, 2,558 each. Option A's is 241,505, which clears the 2028 joint tier-1 threshold of 230,000 → 298.50 Part B + 15.20 Part D = 313.70/month = 3,764 each. Difference: (3,764 − 2,558) × 2 = **2,412**.

## Caveats worth knowing

The engine's sensitivity list flags the one fact that would flip this: at a **4% return** the best choice becomes B (a 1,737 advantage), because less growth means less RMD compression to gain. If the heirs are in the 12% bracket the conversion is worth less (but A still wins), and if Walt dies early the survivor's single brackets actually make converting *more* valuable, not less.

PICK: A
N1: 25492
N2: 2412

## Where they stand in 2026 before any move

Both are 65+, so the standard deduction is $35,500 and the OBBBA senior deduction is the full $12,000 (MAGI is well under $150,000).

| 2026 item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Pension (taxable) | $28,000 |
| Savings interest (6% of $150,000) | $9,000 |
| Non-qualified dividends (10% of $8,550) | $855 |
| Taxable Social Security | $53,694 |
| **AGI** | **$99,244** |
| Taxable income (after $35,500 + $12,000) | $51,744 |
| **Federal tax (option B)** | **$4,790** |

Tax-exempt interest of $20,000 counts in the Pub. 915 worksheet (so taxable SS is $53,694, not the $46,000-ish you'd get ignoring it) and in IRMAA MAGI ($119,244), but not in AGI. Their taxable SS is *not* yet at the 85% ceiling ($58,752), and their 0% capital-gain band runs to $98,900 of taxable income — i.e. about **$47,156 of room**.

## Option A — harvest $110,000 of gains

The gains stack on top of ordinary income, so they blow straight through the 0% band:

- +$11,343 tax on the gains (only ~$42,077 of the $117,695 of gains/qualified dividends stays at 0%; the rest is at 15%)
- +$607 because taxable SS rises $53,694 → $58,752 (the torpedo finishes; you can't dodge it, you just finish it sooner)
- +$926 because the senior deduction shrinks $12,000 → $4,284 (6% of MAGI over $150,000, per person)
- **= $12,876 more federal tax** — about 11.7% of the gain
- And MAGI jumps to $234,302, above the 2028 joint IRMAA tier-1 threshold of $230,000, adding **$2,412** of Part B+D surcharges in 2028.

The raised basis buys them almost nothing: in the projection they never have to sell the brokerage (RMDs plus pension and Social Security cover spending), and the account is held until death, where a basis step-up would wipe out the built-in gain anyway. Net effect: **−$24,478** of after-tax wealth.

## Option C — convert $110,000

Pro-rata on Frank's IRA: the $110,000 comes out after the year's growth, so the nontaxable share is $172,000 / $879,800 = 19.55% → **$21,505 tax-free, $88,495 taxable**.

- +$13,794 tax on the $88,495 of conversion income (12% and 22% brackets)
- +$1,113 finishing the SS torpedo ($53,694 → $58,752)
- +$1,130 senior deduction $12,000 → $6,864
- +$1,154 dividends pushed out of the 0% band
- **= $17,191 more federal tax**, i.e. 15.6% of the $110,000 moved (19.4% of the taxable part)

That is cheap against what the money would otherwise face: the projection has them in the 22% bracket from 2035 on (Frank's first RMD is $57,003 in 2035, $135,139 by 2050), paying NIIT from 2041, and the heirs pay 24% on whatever is left. MAGI of $212,797 also stays *below* the 2028 IRMAA tier-1 threshold, so no premium surcharge. Net effect: **+$39,630** of after-tax wealth, and lifetime tax falls $48,575.

## Answer

After-tax wealth at the end of 2050 in today's dollars: do nothing **$3,163,771**; harvest **$3,139,293**; convert **$3,203,401**. Converting wins by a wide margin — the 0% gain room is real but small (~$47,000), it is being spent on a basis increase they will likely never use, and it drags a 2028 IRMAA surcharge along with it. The conversion uses the same room at ~15.6% to avoid 22–24% later.

The facts that would most change this: the heirs' bracket (at 12% the edge shrinks by ~$12,082), how the accounts are invested (at 8% converting is worth ~$45,626 more), and who dies first (if Joyce dies in 2043 the gain is ~$8,731). Also unstated: how the brokerage is titled, which sets whether the step-up at the first death applies.

PICK: C
N1: 12876
N2: 17191
